newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Gore in South Korea for talks on N.Korea.
newsitem.headline: Gore in South Korea for talks on N.Korea.

text.p: U.S. Vice President Al Gore arrived in Seoul on Friday as U.S. and South Korean officials sought to convince North Korea that "good things will happen" if they enter four-way peace talks.

In its first formal response to a call for peace talks issued in April last year, Pyongyang has indicated it would participate in the talks if the United States and South Korea promised to send supplies to help end its food shortages.
Both Washington and Seoul have been cool to accepting preconditions for the talks, which also would include China.
"The United States and South Korea are not willing to have a precondition for entry into four-party talks," said one senior U.S. official participating in Gore's visit.
"We've told them (North Korea) there will be a great deal of goodwill...if you come into this four-party process. If you come into them, good things will happen," the official said.
Gore, fresh from a five-day visit in China, planned to discuss the four-way talks during a meeting on Saturday with South Korean President Kim Young-sam.

"Our two nations and our two peoples have been allies for nearly half a century, standing watch together here for the causes of peace, security and stability," Gore said during toasts at a Friday evening dinner hosted by Prime Minister Koh Kun.
Stressing the U.S. commitment to Seoul, Gore told his host that "the growth of your democracy has made our alliance even closer".
The prime minister praised Gore and said his eight-day trip to the region, which included a visit to Japan, "signifies the bonds between the United States and this region".

Immediately after arriving in Seoul, Gore went to the national cemetery where he honoured the 160,000 South Korean war dead buried there. During a simple but moving ceremony, he placed a wreath at a memorial and added three pinches of incense to an eternal flame.
An important aspect of Gore's mission was to discuss latest efforts to convince North Korea to enter the four-way talks.

The talks would be aimed initially at securing a lasting peace to replace the armistice that ended the 1950-1953 Korean War, which the United States believes would serve as a spring board for ending tensions on the peninsula.

After his talks on Saturday with Kim at the presidential Blue House, Gore was to visit the Demilitarized Zone separating the North and South and meet some of the 37,000 U.S. troops stationed in South Korea.

International aid agencies say North Korea, devastated by two consecutive years of floods, is weeks away from starvation. Seoul officials say that by linking food aid to the talks, Pyongyang had revealed its desperation.
U.S. officials travelling with Gore said the vice-president discussed the four-way talks during his closed-door meetings in Beijing with President Jiang Zemin and Prime Minister Li Peng.
The officials declined to discuss the private conversations, but one official said: "We are hopeful things are moving in the right direction."
Meanwhile, five U.S. senators headed to Pyongyang on Friday after a three-day visit to South Korea.

The delegation led by Ted Stevens, the chairman of the Senate Appropriations Committee, met with Kim before departing on their mission. Accompanying Stevens were Republicans Pete Domenici of New Mexico, Thad Cochran of Mississippi, Pat Roberts of Kansas and Democrat Daniel Inouye of Hawaii.
